Git is a tool that keeps selected versions of a project so you can inspect an earlier version or restore its file contents later. It records a snapshot of the project each time you deliberately make a record called a commit. Saving a file in your editor does not make a commit, and Git does not automatically record every edit.

Imagine you are making a digital painting. You finish the outline, prepare that version for Git to record, and make a commit. Later, you add a blue sky and prepare and commit that version too. The blue sky commit keeps the earlier outline in the project's history. If you then try an orange sky and prefer the blue one, you can inspect or restore the recorded blue sky version.

The useful distinction is between the file you are currently editing and the versions you have deliberately recorded. New commits normally add to the history while keeping earlier commits available. That lets you keep developing the painting without losing its recorded stages, but it does not guarantee that an unrecorded edit can be recovered.
